jsonld.name: Egyptian Koshari
jsonld.description: Koshari is Cairo on a plate: rice, lentils, and macaroni sharing a bowl with chickpeas, drowned in a spiced tomato sauce, crowned with a storm of crispy fried onions, and dressed at the last second with a vinegar-chile cut sharp enough to carry the whole carbohydrate nation on its back. It is the street food of the republic — assembled in vast copper basins in alleys off Midan Talaat Harb, served in seconds, costing almost nothing — and it is, quietly, one of the great vegetarian dishes on earth. No meat, no stock, no dairy: only grain and legume and allium, engineered into complete satisfaction.

skeleton:
Egyptian Koshari

Egyptian · Medium · Serves 6

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Koshari is Cairo on a plate: rice, lentils, and macaroni sharing a bowl with chickpeas, drowned in a spiced tomato sauce, crowned with a storm of crispy fried onions, and dressed at the last second with a vinegar-chile cut sharp enough to carry the whole carbohydrate nation on its back. It is the street food of the republic — assembled in vast copper basins in alleys off Midan Talaat Harb, served in seconds, costing almost nothing — and it is, quietly, one of the great vegetarian dishes on earth. No meat, no stock, no dairy: only grain and legume and allium, engineered into complete satisfaction.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The grains and legumes

The sauce

The crispy onions (the crown — non-negotiable)

The finishing sauce (daqqah — the sharp cut)

- **Cook each element separately and season each one.** Koshari is not a stew; it is five preparations meeting in a bowl, and each must taste complete alone — the lentils salted with cumin, the rice toasted with vermicelli, the pasta properly salted, the sauce balanced, the onions shattering. The assembly is the diner's or the server's; the kitchen's work is the parts. - **The bridge:** the Egyptian pantry here is cumin, garlic, tomato, and vinegar — nothing exotic. The one true ingredient is patience with the onions; the crispy crown is the dish's soul, and the shallow-pan method (onions fried patiently in 1 cm of oil, drained, salted) delivers it without a deep fryer.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The parts: lentils intact, rice toasted and separate, pasta salted, sauce cooked past its acid.
  • The onions: snapped-crisp, salted, crowned last.
  • The bowl: layers distinct, daqqah at the table.

Egyptian Koshari

Prep: 40 minutes · Cook: 50 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 35 minutes · Serves 6

Ingredients

The grains and legumes

  • 200 g brown or green lentils, picked over
  • 200 g long-grain rice, rinsed; 50 g vermicelli or small macaroni broken short
  • 150 g elbow macaroni (the street runs both pastas; one is honest)
  • 1 can (400 g) chickpeas, drained, or 200 g cooked
  • 2 tsp cumin, divided; salt

The sauce

  • 3 tbsp neutral oil; 1 onion (about 150 g), minced
  • 6 cloves garlic (about 25 g), minced; 1 tbsp tomato paste (about 15 g)
  • 800 g crushed tomatoes or tomato passata
  • 2 tsp cumin; 1 tsp coriander; ½ tsp chile flakes (or 1 tsp harissa, #91)
  • 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp sugar; a splash of water as needed

The crispy onions (the crown — non-negotiable)

  • 3 large onions (about 500 g), sliced thin
  • Neutral oil for frying, 1 cm deep at 175 °C; or the shallow-pan method below
  • A pinch of salt

The finishing sauce (daqqah — the sharp cut)

  • 4 tbsp white or apple-cider vinegar (about 60 ml); 2 tbsp water
  • 4 cloves garlic, minced fine; 1–2 tsp chile flakes or 1 tsp harissa
  • ½ tsp cumin; a pinch of salt

Instructions

  1. **The lentils and the rice (35 minutes).** Simmer the lentils in salted water with 1 tsp cumin until tender but intact — 20–25 minutes; drain. In a pot, toast the vermicelli in 2 tbsp oil to deep gold, add the rinsed rice and a further 2 minutes of toasting, then salted water (1:1.5 rice to water), cover, and cook 15 minutes off the flame's residual heat. Checkpoint — the lentils must hold their shape — mushy lentils collapse the bowl's layers. The vermicelli should be a shade darker than feels safe; its toast is the rice's flavor.
  2. **The sauce (30 minutes at a murmur).** Soften the onion in the oil, add the garlic and tomato paste and fry 2 minutes to darken, then the tomatoes, spices, salt, and sugar. Simmer gently, half-covered, until the sauce thickens and darkens — the raw-acid edge cooked out — about 25 minutes. Checkpoint — taste: the sauce should be savory-sweet with cumin's warmth, noticeably seasoned — it must sauce a mountain of starch. Blend half for smoothness if you like the street's texture; leave half rustic.
  3. **The onions (15–20 minutes, watched).** Fry the sliced onions in the oil over medium-high, stirring, until they pass pale, pass golden, and reach a deep even crisp brown — this last stage takes courage; the line between crisp and burnt is under a minute. Drain on paper, salt immediately. Make the daqqah by warming its elements together for 2 minutes off any real heat. Checkpoint — a cooled onion strand should snap, not bend. They crisp further as they cool — pull them one shade before the target color.
  4. **Assembly — the layering, in order, per bowl.** A base of rice, lentils spooned over, macaroni next, chickpeas scattered, the hot sauce ladled generously, the crispy onions piled on in a golden heap — and the daqqah dashed over by the diner's hand at the table. Checkpoint — eating test: the first spoonful runs the full stack — soft rice, earthy lentil, giving pasta, the sauce's tomato-cumin warmth — then the onions shatter through everything, and the daqqah's vinegar-garlic fire lands at the swallow. Each element should stay distinct in the bowl: koshari is layered, never mixed until the spoon does the mixing. The crispy onions must survive the sauce's steam, which is why the crown goes on at the last second — and why the second bowl is always better planned than executed.

Finish & Plate

Served in wide bowls, the onions' gold crown over the sauce's red — a dish whose appearance is its recipe. Extra daqqah and hot sauce at the table for the fire-eaters; a spoon deep enough to reach the bottom in one pass.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Bowl heavy, monotoneDaqqah skippedThe vinegar cut is structural — never omit
Onions gone softCrowned under hot sauce too earlyLast-second crowning; extra batch if needed
Lentils mushyOver-boiled or soaked long20–25 minutes checked, drained at intact

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- Every component keeps 3 days refrigerated separately — koshari is the original meal-prep street food; reheat each element and assemble to order. The onions keep 2 days airtight at room temperature and re-crisp 2 minutes in a 180 °C oven. - Variations: the Alexandrian school runs a spicier sauce; the home versions add fried liver for the meat eaters. The #18 lablabi is koshari's Tunisian cousin — the same grain-and-cumin instinct on a different base.
